# Part I: Conceptual Foundations

---

## Why Data Analytics in Pure & Applied Sciences?

Data analysis transforms raw laboratory measurements, survey responses, and experimental observations into **actionable scientific insight**.

::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="50%"}
### Common Challenges
* Small sample sizes ($n < 30$)
* Non-normal laboratory readings
* Distinguishing signal from experimental noise
* Selecting the wrong test for nominal vs. continuous metrics
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
### Strategic Goal
To equip researchers across **Microbiology, Chemistry, Physics, Hospitality, and Food Science** with standard, reproducible statistical techniques.
:::

:::

---

## Understanding Data Types

Before choosing a statistical test, you **must** identify your measurement scale:


```

```
                        Data Types
                            │
     ┌──────────────────────┴──────────────────────┐
Quantitative                                  Qualitative

```

(Numeric / Continuous)                      (Categorical / Discrete)
│                                             │
┌────┴──────────────┐                     ┌────────┴────────────┐
Continuous          Discrete              Nominal               Ordinal
(pH, Yield, Temp)   (Cell counts)       (Sample Types)       (Likert scale)

```

> **Rule of Thumb:** Your data type directly dictates whether you apply parametric tests (e.g., $t$-test, ANOVA) or non-parametric tests (e.g., Mann-Whitney, Kruskal-Wallis).

---

## Formulating Scientific Hypotheses

Every statistical test starts with two competing hypotheses:

### 1. Null Hypothesis ($H_0$)
* Statement of **no difference**, **no effect**, or **no association**.
* *Example (Food Tech):* $H_0$: Shelf-life duration does not differ across three storage packaging materials.

### 2. Alternative Hypothesis ($H_1$ or $H_a$)
* Statement of **an effect**, **a difference**, or **a relationship**.
* *Example (Food Tech):* $H_1$: At least one packaging material yields a significantly different shelf-life duration.

---

## Statistical Test Selection Matrix

| Research Question | Input (X) | Output (Y) | Parametric Test | Non-Parametric Equivalent |
|:---|:---|:---|:---|:---|
| Compare 2 independent groups | Categorical (2 levels) | Continuous (Normal) | **Independent $t$-test** | Mann-Whitney U test |
| Compare 2 paired measurements | Categorical (Paired) | Continuous (Normal) | **Paired $t$-test** | Wilcoxon signed-rank |
| Compare 3+ groups | Categorical (3+ levels)| Continuous (Normal) | **One-Way ANOVA** | Kruskal-Wallis test |
| Assess linear relationship | Continuous | Continuous | **Pearson Correlation** | Spearman Correlation |
| Predict continuous response | Continuous/Categorical | Continuous | **Linear Regression** | Generalized Linear Models |

---

## Interpreting the $p$-value and $R^2$

### The $p$-value
* Measures the probability of observing your data under $H_0$.
* Standard Threshold ($\alpha = 0.05$):
  * **$p < 0.05$**: Reject $H_0 \rightarrow$ Statistically significant effect.
  * **$p \ge 0.05$**: Fail to reject $H_0 \rightarrow$ Insufficient evidence.

### Coefficient of Determination ($R^2$)
* Quantifies the proportion of variance in $Y$ explained by model $X$.
* *Example:* $R^2 = 0.84 \implies$ 84% of product viscosity change is explained by temperature variation.

# Part II: Hands-on Analysis in R

---

## Environment Setup & Package Loading

```r
# Load required libraries for the session
library(tidyverse)  # Data manipulation and ggplot2 visualization
library(ggpubr)     # Publication-ready plots and statistical annotations
library(rstatix)    # Pipe-friendly statistical testing framework

# Set global ggplot theme
theme_set(theme_minimal(base_size = 14))

```

---

## Generating Multidisciplinary Sample Data

```r
# Simulate experimental research data across SPAS disciplines
set.seed(2026)

research_data <- tibble(
  Sample_ID = 1:60,
  Department = rep(c("Food_Science", "Applied_Chem", "Microbiology"), each = 20),
  Treatment_Temp = rep(c(25, 45, 65, 85), times = 15),
  Enzyme_Activity = round(c(
    rnorm(20, mean = 45, sd = 5),
    rnorm(20, mean = 62, sd = 6),
    rnorm(20, mean = 55, sd = 4)
  ), 2)
)

head(research_data, 5)

```

---

## Summary Statistics by Department

```r
# Calculate summary metrics (Mean, SD, Median, IQR)
summary_table <- research_data %>%
  group_by(Department) %>%
  get_summary_stats(Enzyme_Activity, type = "common")

summary_table

```

---

## Exploratory Data Visualization

```r
# Visualizing distributions across departments
ggplot(research_data, aes(x = Department, y = Enzyme_Activity, fill = Department)) +
  geom_boxplot(alpha = 0.7, outlier.colour = "red") +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.1, alpha = 0.5) +
  labs(
    title = "Enzyme Activity Distribution Across SPAS Departments",
    x = "Department Group",
    y = "Enzyme Activity (U/mL)"
  ) +
  theme(legend.position = "none")

```

---

# Part III: Inferential Statistics & Modeling

---

## Evaluating Group Differences (One-Way ANOVA)

### Research Question

Does mean **Enzyme Activity** differ significantly across the three departments?

```r
# Compute One-Way ANOVA
anova_res <- research_data %>%
  anova_test(Enzyme_Activity ~ Department)

anova_res

```

---

## Post-Hoc Pairwise Comparisons

If ANOVA indicates significant differences ($p < 0.05$), execute Tukey HSD post-hoc testing:

```r
# Pairwise comparisons with p-value adjustment
post_hoc <- research_data %>%
  tukey_hsd(Enzyme_Activity ~ Department)

post_hoc %>%
  select(group1, group2, p.adj, p.adj.signif)

```

---

## Regression Analysis: Predicting Yield

```r
# Fitting a linear regression model
fit_model <- lm(Enzyme_Activity ~ Treatment_Temp, data = research_data)

# Display model summary
summary(fit_model)

```

---

## Visualizing Regression Trends

```r
ggplot(research_data, aes(x = Treatment_Temp, y = Enzyme_Activity)) +
  geom_point(color = "#2b5c8f", size = 3) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", color = "#d9534f", se = TRUE) +
  stat_regline_equation(label.x = 30, label.y = 75) +
  stat_cor(label.x = 30, label.y = 70) +
  labs(
    title = "Effect of Temperature on Enzyme Activity",
    x = "Temperature (°C)",
    y = "Enzyme Activity (U/mL)"
  )

```

---

## Practical Takeaways for Researchers

1. **Know Your Data:** Categorical vs. Continuous determines your analytical pathway.
2. **Check Assumptions:** Always verify normality and homogeneity of variance before parametric tests.
3. **Focus on Interpretation:** Report effect size and confidence intervals alongside $p$-values.
4. **Reproducibility:** Use Quarto documents (`.qmd`) to bundle code, outputs, and scientific write-ups together.
